CORRELATIONS

Correlations and joint probability

Dependence between candidate legs, measured from official game data with sample sizes and confidence intervals - and, equally important, an explicit account of what cannot be measured.

Why correlations decide whether a parlay is a strategy

Two legs that each look like 60% plays are a 36% parlay only if the legs are independent. If they move together the true probability is higher; if one suppresses the other it is lower. Pricing a parlay as a product of marginals is the most common way a multi-leg system silently loses money, which is why gate G7 forbids a combination whose legs have not been measured.
